scenes.name: the register file and the trade
scenes.visual: A diagram of the register file. Arithmetic units connect directly to named register slots with single-cycle access. A partitioning chart illustrates the trade: 256 KB divided by 4 bytes yields 65,536 registers. Allocating 32 per thread allows 2,048 threads; allocating 64 halves occupancy to 1,024.

beats.say: An arithmetic unit cannot reach into memory. It can only read from a register and write to a register.
beats.show: A diagram shows memory on the far right and the math unit on the left. Between them sit named register slots 'r0', 'r1', 'r2'. An arrow shows the required path: memory into register, register into math unit.

beats.say: The register step is not optional. Every number must land in a register before the maths can touch it.
beats.show: A direct path from memory to arithmetic flashes red with a prohibition icon, then redirects cleanly through register r0.

beats.say: Each multiprocessor contains two hundred and fifty-six kilobytes of registers, giving sixty-five thousand five hundred and thirty-six slots.
beats.show: A large register bank lights up: '256 KB ÷ 4 bytes = 65,536 registers'. Access time highlights: 'single-cycle access'.

beats.say: Those registers are partitioned across resident threads. Give each thread thirty-two registers, and all two thousand and forty-eight threads fit.
beats.show: A horizontal bar splits into 2,048 slices: '32 registers per thread · 100% occupancy (2,048 threads)'.

beats.say: Double the registers to sixty-four, and only half as many threads fit. Hoarding registers buys speed per thread, but leaves fewer threads to hide memory waits.
beats.show: The allocation bar adjusts to 64 registers per thread: occupancy drops to 50% (1,024 threads). At 128 registers, it drops to 25%. Takeaway: 'registers per thread trade one-for-one with occupancy'.

scenes.name: on-chip S RAM and the scratchpad
scenes.visual: A schematic of the 256 KB SRAM block on the multiprocessor. A configurable slider splits the block between hardware L1 cache and software-managed shared memory (up to 228 KB).

beats.say: Beside the registers sits another two hundred and fifty-six kilobytes of fast S RAM.
beats.show: A 256 KB memory block highlights on the multiprocessor die labeled '256 KB on-chip SRAM'.

beats.say: The programmer can claim up to two hundred and twenty-eight kilobytes of this as shared memory, a scratchpad managed by software.
beats.show: A divider slides across the block: 228 KB fills in teal labeled 'shared memory scratchpad (explicit code control)'.

beats.say: Whatever is not claimed serves as an automatic L one cache.
beats.show: The remaining portion fills in grey: 'automatic L1 cache (hardware managed)'. Takeaway: 'the split between cache and scratchpad is chosen by software'.

scenes.name: tiling: why staging saves memory traffic
scenes.visual: A matrix multiply of a 4x4 output tile (16 threads). Without staging, each thread reads its 8 inputs from HBM (128 total reads). With staging, the 16 numbers of A and 16 of B are copied into shared memory once (32 total reads), cutting HBM traffic fourfold.

beats.say: Shared memory exists to enable tiling: staging data so cooperating threads can share it without hitting memory.
beats.show: A 4 by 4 output grid C appears (16 cells, 16 threads). Above it sits tile B; to its left sits tile A.

beats.say: Each output cell needs four numbers from row A and four numbers from column B, eight numbers in all.
beats.show: Output cell c23 highlights, showing its dot product requiring row 2 of A (4 values) and column 3 of B (4 values).

beats.say: If all sixteen threads fetched their own eight numbers from memory, the block would make a hundred and twenty-eight reads.
beats.show: 16 threads send independent arrows down to HBM. Read counter increments to '16 threads × 8 reads = 128 reads from HBM'.

beats.say: Instead, the block copies the sixteen numbers of A and sixteen of B into shared memory once, making thirty-two reads in all.
beats.show: The block performs 32 collaborative reads from HBM into the shared memory scratchpad. Read counter drops: '32 reads from HBM'.

beats.say: Every thread then reads from shared memory. That is four times fewer reads, exactly the width of the tile. A tile a hundred and twenty-eight wide saves a hundred and twenty-eight times.
beats.show: Threads read freely from the shared scratchpad. A comparison card shows: '128 reads unstaged vs 32 reads staged: 4× saving'. Takeaway: 'tiling trades on-chip scratchpad space for a massive reduction in memory traffic'.

scenes.name: cache versus shared memory
scenes.visual: A side-by-side comparison of automatic cache versus explicit shared memory. A token generation stream shows weights passing through once, demonstrating why automatic caching fails for autoregressive decode.

beats.say: A cache is simply a small, fast copy of something slow and far away. It works only when programs reuse data.
beats.show: A small cache box sits beside a large memory store. Repeated requests hit the cache in teal.

beats.say: A program that touches every number exactly once gains nothing from any cache, however large. Generating one token touches every weight once.
beats.show: A stream of weights flows past the cache. Each weight is touched once and discarded; by the time it could be reused, thousands of other weights have evicted it.

beats.say: Both cache and shared memory use the same physical silicon. The difference is who decides what is in them.
beats.show: Two cards appear: left 'Hardware cache · hardware guesses based on recency'; right 'Shared memory · software explicitly stages blocks'.

beats.say: When streaming through weights, guessing is useless. Stating exactly which tiles to stage is everything.
beats.show: The shared memory card glows teal. Takeaway pill: 'caches rely on luck; shared memory relies on explicit engineering'.

checks.claim: 256 KB register file / 4 bytes per register = 65,536 registers
Unstaged 4x4 tile reads: 16 threads * 8 reads = 128 reads
Staged 4x4 tile reads: 16 of A + 16 of B = 32 reads
Tiling saving ratio: 128 / 32 = 4x saving (equal to tile width 4)
